tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Active vocabulary differs from passive vocabulary in that active vocabulary is:
options: Words we use in speaking and writing, while passive vocabulary is words we understand but rarely use

questions.question_text: Vocabulary development is important for business because it:
options: Improves clarity, precision and professional impression in communication
questions.explanation: The right word saves time and avoids misunderstanding.

questions.question_text: Prefixes are:
options: Letters added at the beginning of a word to change its meaning, e.g., un-, re-, dis-, pre-, mis-

questions.question_text: Suffixes are:
options: Letters added at the end of a word to form new words, e.g., -tion, -ment, -ness, -able, -ful
questions.explanation: They often change the part of speech.

questions.question_text: A root word is:
options: The basic part of a word that carries its core meaning, e.g., "act" in action, active, actor
questions.explanation: Words formed from it make a word family.

questions.question_text: The roots bene, mal, port, dict and graph mean:
options: Good, bad, carry, say and write
questions.explanation: E.g., benefit, malfunction, transport, dictate, photograph.

questions.question_text: Adding -tion, -ment, -ness, -able and -ful respectively to "act/ manage/ kind/ break/ care" can give:
A word family of "decide" includes:
Compounding is:
options: Joining two words to form a new word, e.g., notebook, bookshelf, headline
questions.explanation: Compounds may be written as one word, hyphenated or separate.

questions.question_text: Synonyms of "big", "buy" and "begin" are:
Antonyms of "expand", "scarce" and "accept" are:
Homophones are words that:
options: Sound the same but have different meanings and spellings, e.g., "write" and "right"

questions.question_text: Homonyms are words that:
options: Have the same spelling or sound but different meanings, e.g., "bank" (river or money)

questions.question_text: Collocations are:
options: Words that commonly go together, e.g., "make a decision", "meet a deadline"

questions.question_text: "Break the ice" means:
options: To start a conversation and ease tension
questions.explanation: It is used in social and business settings.

questions.question_text: "Bite the bullet" means:
options: To face a difficult situation bravely
questions.explanation: It means to endure something unpleasant.

questions.question_text: "A blessing in disguise" means:
options: Something that seems bad but turns out good
questions.explanation: E.g., losing a job that leads to a better one.

questions.question_text: "Back to square one" means:
questions.explanation: It is used when efforts fail.

questions.question_text: "Cut corners" means:
options: To do something in the cheapest or quickest way, often sacrificing quality

questions.question_text: "In the red" means:
options: Owing money or making a loss
questions.explanation: It comes from red ink for losses.

questions.question_text: "The ball is in your court" means:
options: It is your turn to take action or decide

questions.question_text: "Spill the beans" means:
questions.explanation: It is used for disclosing secrets.

questions.question_text: "Think outside the box" means:
"On the same page" means:
options: To be in the same room
To share the same understanding or agreement

questions.question_text: Which sentence uses "hit the nail on the head" correctly?
options: "She hit the nail on the head with joy."
"He hit the nail on the head by mistake."
"Your analysis of the problem hit the nail on the head."
questions.explanation: It means to describe something exactly right.

tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: The phrasal verbs "set up", "carry out" and "call off" mean:
questions.explanation: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle.

questions.question_text: "Look into" means:
questions.explanation: "The team will look into the complaint."

questions.question_text: "Turn down" means:
"Come up with" means:
options: To think of or produce an idea

questions.question_text: The one word for "a person who loves books" is:
The one word for "agreed by all" is:
The one word for "present everywhere" is:
The one word for "a life story written by oneself" is:
questions.explanation: A biography is written by another person.

questions.question_text: The one word for "of unknown authorship" is:
questions.explanation: Anonymous means without a known name.

questions.question_text: The one word for "one who helps mankind" is:
The one word for "exclusive control of the market" is:
questions.explanation: It means a single seller controls the market.

questions.question_text: The one word for "that which cannot be avoided" is:
Revenue, turnover, dividend, asset and liability are, respectively:
options: Income earned; total sales; share of profit paid to shareholders; resource owned; obligation owed

questions.question_text: A stakeholder is _____, and a merger is _____:
options: An owner only; the splitting of a company
Anyone affected by or interested in a business; the combining of two companies
questions.explanation: Acquisition is one company taking over another.

questions.question_text: "Adapt" differs from "adopt" in that "adapt" means _____ and "adopt" means _____:
options: To adjust to new conditions; to take up or accept

questions.question_text: "Continual" differs from "continuous" in that "continual" means _____ and "continuous" means _____:
options: Repeated at intervals; without a break

questions.question_text: "Eminent" differs from "imminent" in that "eminent" means _____ and "imminent" means _____:
options: Famous or respected; about to happen

questions.question_text: "Farther" differs from "further" in that "farther" is used for _____ and "further" for _____:
Denotation is _____, and connotation is _____:
options: The literal dictionary meaning; the emotional or cultural associations
The emotional meaning; the dictionary meaning
questions.explanation: "Home" denotes a house but connotes warmth.

questions.question_text: Formal register differs from informal register in that formal language:
options: Uses polished vocabulary and avoids contractions, e.g., "I would like to enquire" instead of "I wanna ask"

questions.question_text: Ways of building vocabulary include:
options: Reading widely, using a dictionary, learning words in context and revising regularly
questions.explanation: Using new words in speech also helps.

questions.question_text: To use a dictionary effectively, you should:
options: Check meaning, pronunciation, part of speech and example sentences
Look only at the first meaning

questions.question_text: A thesaurus should be used carefully because:
options: Synonyms are not always interchangeable in meaning or tone
questions.explanation: Check the usage of the chosen word.

questions.question_text: Spaced repetition is:
options: Revising words at increasing intervals to improve memory

questions.question_text: Learning words in context helps because:
options: It shows how a word is used, its meaning and collocations

tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: The stress in "product" (noun) and "produce" (verb) is respectively on:
options: The first syllable (PROduct) and the second syllable (proDUCE)

questions.question_text: Intonation is:
options: The rise and fall of the voice in speech; rising intonation is used for yes/no questions
questions.explanation: Falling intonation is used for statements.

questions.question_text: Which word has a silent letter?
questions.explanation: Other examples: hour, psychology, write, listen.

questions.question_text: A dialogue is:
options: A conversation between two or more people
questions.explanation: It can be written or spoken.

questions.question_text: The purpose of dialogue writing is to:
options: Show how people speak and interact, and develop communication skills

questions.question_text: The format of a dialogue includes:
options: Speaker names followed by a colon and their words, on separate lines
questions.explanation: Each turn starts on a new line.

questions.question_text: A rule of dialogue writing is:
options: Keep the sentences short, natural and appropriate to the speakers and context
questions.explanation: Each speaker should have a clear role.

questions.question_text: Expressions for agreeing, disagreeing, suggesting and apologising respectively are:
A formal dialogue opens with a _____ and closes with a _____:
options: Polite greeting; courteous thanks or farewell
questions.explanation: "Good morning, sir… Thank you for your time."

questions.question_text: A formal dialogue differs from an informal dialogue in that a formal dialogue:
options: Uses polite, standard language, while an informal one uses casual language

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a customer and a bank officer on opening an account, the officer would most likely say:
options: "Good morning, how may I help you? Please fill in this form and attach your KYC documents."

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between two colleagues on a project deadline, a suitable line is:
options: "We need to finish the report by Friday; can you share the data today?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a teacher and a student on a missed assignment, a suitable student line is:
options: "I'm sorry, ma'am. I was ill; may I submit it tomorrow?"
questions.explanation: It is polite and gives a reason.

questions.question_text: In an interview dialogue, a suitable candidate line is:
options: "Thank you for the opportunity. I have studied accounting and completed an internship."

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a shopkeeper and a customer on a discount, a suitable customer line is:
options: "Could you offer a discount if I buy two?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue with a customer-care executive about a damaged product, a suitable customer line is:
options: "The product arrived damaged; I would like a replacement, please."
questions.explanation: It states the problem and the request.

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between two friends planning a trip, a suitable line is:
options: "Let's go to Goa in December; what's our budget?"

questions.question_text: A telephone dialogue between a receptionist and a caller typically begins with:
options: "Good morning, ABC Company, how may I help you?"
questions.explanation: It is a polite standard opening.

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a manager and an employee seeking leave, a suitable employee line is:
options: "May I request leave from 10 to 12 October for a family function?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a doctor and a patient, a suitable doctor line is:
options: "What symptoms are you having, and since when?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a salesperson and a client on a new product, a suitable salesperson line is:
options: "Our new model is lighter and more energy-efficient; may I show you a demonstration?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between two students on exam preparation, a suitable line is:
options: "Shall we revise the ledger chapter together tonight?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between an insurance agent and a customer, a suitable agent line is:
options: "This plan gives you life cover of Rs 10 lakh for a small annual premium."

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a travel agent and a customer booking a ticket, a suitable agent line is:
options: "Which date would you like to travel, and do you prefer a window seat?"

questions.question_text: In a dialogue between a manager and a team about an urgent change in plan, a suitable manager line is:
options: "The client has moved the deadline up to Monday, so we must reorganise our tasks today."

tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Storytelling is:
options: The art of narrating events to engage and communicate a message
questions.explanation: Its purposes include entertaining, teaching and persuading.

questions.question_text: The elements of a story are:
options: Characters, setting, plot, conflict and theme

questions.question_text: Plot, conflict, climax and resolution mean respectively:
options: The problem; the outcome; the sequence; the climax
The climax; the plot; the resolution; the conflict
The sequence of events; the problem; the turning point; the outcome
The outcome; the sequence; the problem; the turning point
questions.explanation: Together they make the story's arc.

questions.question_text: Freytag's pyramid has the stages:
options: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution

questions.question_text: The hero's journey is:
options: A story pattern in which a hero leaves home, faces challenges and returns changed

questions.question_text: The point of view in a story is:
options: The perspective from which it is told, such as first person or third person

questions.question_text: "Show" differs from "tell" in that "show" uses:
options: Vivid details and actions, while "tell" states facts directly
questions.explanation: "Her hands trembled" shows nervousness; "she was nervous" tells it.

questions.question_text: Storytelling techniques include:
options: Hook, vivid details, dialogue, suspense and emotion

questions.question_text: A story with the moral "Honesty is the best policy" would most likely show:
options: A character who tells the truth and is rewarded or trusted
A character who lies and succeeds

questions.question_text: A story with the moral "Unity is strength" would most likely show:
options: Characters working together and succeeding where they failed alone

questions.question_text: The best continuation of "The lights went out and then…" is:
options: …a faint knock echoed through the dark house.

questions.question_text: A short story on "A small act of kindness" would most likely show:
options: A simple helpful gesture that makes a big difference to someone

questions.question_text: A story from a customer's point of view is told:
options: In the first person ("I") or from the customer's perspective

questions.question_text: To deliver a story orally, you should:
options: Use voice modulation, pauses, gestures and eye contact

questions.question_text: The role of voice modulation and pauses in storytelling is to:
Business storytelling is:
options: Using stories to communicate ideas, brand values or data in presentations, marketing and leadership

questions.question_text: The STAR method stands for:
Storytelling helps in interviews by:
options: Illustrating skills with real examples in a clear structure

questions.question_text: Storytelling helps in a sales pitch by:
options: Connecting emotionally with the client and showing the product's value through a relatable story
questions.explanation: Stories are more memorable than facts alone.

questions.question_text: A tip for effective storytelling is to:
options: Know your audience, keep a clear structure and be authentic

questions.question_text: A way to overcome nervousness while speaking is:
options: Prepare well, practise, breathe deeply and focus on the message

questions.question_text: Filler words such as "um", "like" and "you know" can be reduced by:
options: Pausing silently, practising and slowing down

questions.question_text: Active listening means:
options: Fully concentrating, understanding and responding to the speaker
questions.explanation: It includes nodding, paraphrasing and asking questions.

questions.question_text: Body language is important while speaking because it:
options: Reinforces or contradicts the spoken message and builds credibility
questions.explanation: Posture, gestures and eye contact matter.

questions.question_text: A short speech is structured as:
options: Opening (hook), body (2–3 key points) and conclusion (summary/call to action)
